title: How To Turn On Developer Mode On Your Chromebook
excerpt: ChromeOS has a lot of safety guardrails, but for those who want to step outside their Chromebook's standard uses, enabling Developer Mode might be necessary.
content_html:
It's easy, but it's also a little risky.

Savusia Konstantin/Getty Images

Chromebooks have earned their reputation as affordable, secure and simple machines over the years. Most owners never venture beyond the Play Store, downloading apps and calling it a day. But much like Android power users, Chromebook owners can take things one step further and unlock a completely different experience by turning on Developer Mode.

Developer Mode strips away many of ChromeOS' built-in protections and gives you full control over the system, which may or may not be a good idea depending on your technical knowledge. Still, you get root access, kernel modifications and the ability to install software that was never on the Play Store. It's a powerful tool, so it's not something you should use without understanding what you're getting into.

So what exactly does Developer Mode do? When does it actually make sense to use it? How do you enable this feature? We'll dig through everything and discuss what changes once Developer Mode is on and whether it's something you need as you use your Chromebook as your everyday computer.

What is Developer Mode on a Chromebook?

CC Photo Labs/Shutterstock

Developer Mode is a system setting that gives you more control over how your device operates, relaxing ChromeOS' "verified boot" protections. Normally, ChromeOS runs on a locked-down system. It double-checks itself on every boot, reverting automatically if something looks tampered with and sandboxing every app and webpage so problems can't spread. Developer Mode tears down most of those protections.

As with most systems, once Developer Mode is enabled, you gain full system access. That means you can change the ChromeOS kernel and core files. The trade-off is security. With Verified Boot relaxed, your Chromebook no longer has some of its default defenses against malicious tampering. Lest you forget you made this move, there'll be a visual reminder in the form of a warning screen on startup that reads OS Verification is OFF or You are in Developer Mode. The warning times out after 30 seconds with a warning beep, so there's no way to say you didn't know. It's not a sign of danger, but it's a signal that your system is running without a safety net.

When would you actually need Developer Mode?

Lenovo

Let's be honest here: Developer Mode isn't something the average Chromebook owner needs to think about. Most day-to-day tasks like shooting emails, browsing, streaming, editing documents and so on work just fine within the safety brackets provided by stock ChromeOS.

That said, there are situations when enabling Developer Mode is needed. For instance, while modern ChromeOS includes built-in support for running Linux apps in a secure sandbox, deeper system-level modifications still require Developer Mode. You'll need it if you want full root shell access to the OS, need to load custom Linux kernels or plan to run alternative operating systems. Developer Mode is also required for advanced system tweaks like firmware modifications and boot flag changes.

Also, if you want to quickly double-click and install APK files directly through the native ChromeOS Files app without touching the command line, Developer Mode is required. It's worth noting that ChromeOS now allows you to sideload APKs securely without Developer Mode by enabling Android Debug Bridge inside the official Linux environment. If that's the reason you're looking into Developer Mode, you might want to try this out first.

Of course, Developer Mode is also going to be a feature that actual developers building or debugging apps for ChromeOS might use. If none of these apply to you, there's a strong chance you should leave your Chromebook alone. Note that school- or work-managed Chromebooks usually have Developer Mode blocked by the administrator.

How to turn on Developer Mode

CL Shebley/Shutterstock

If you still want to turn on Developer Mode, then you need to follow a few steps. One important thing to know is that switching between Normal and Developer Mode wipes all local user data.

  1. Let's boot the system into Recovery Mode. Press and hold Esc + Refresh + Power simultaneously to do this on a standard Chromebook laptop.

  2. From the Recovery screen, press Ctrl + D and confirm the prompt that pops up asking whether you want to turn OS Verification off. The system will then reboot.

  3. Next, you'll see one of two notifications: "You are in Developer Mode" or "OS Verification is OFF" (the exact wording can vary by device). Press Ctrl + D to start the transition right away, or just wait 30 seconds for the beep and it will begin on its own. This is when the local data gets wiped. The process can take up to 15 minutes, so do not interrupt it.

Developer Mode transforms a Chromebook from a simplified, locked-down device into a system that's a lot easier to customize. The cost, however, is your device's security — one of the things that make ChromeOS appealing in the first place, especially for people who were hoping to get an affordable Chromebook to use as their daily driver. For developers or Linux enthusiasts, however, it's a genuinely useful tool. If you decide to enable it, back up your files first, keep your device plugged in and follow the steps carefully.
